title: Why App.net bet on paid, ad-free services: Dalton Caldwell's case against ad-supported products
summary: Dalton argues that services too important to their users (SourceForge/GitHub, Dropbox) shouldn't be ad-supported, and that paid, profitable stewards build better products. Drawing on his imeem failure, he proposes a Kickstarter-style campaign requiring $500K / ~10,000 backers as critical mass before App.net launches a paid realtime feed service.

principles.text: Services that are too important to users shouldn't be ad-supported; charge for them instead.
principles.quote: the services provided by SourceForge/Github are **too important to its users to be ad-supported**.

principles.text: A paid, profitable steward builds a better product than an ad-supported one, because the team improves the service instead of extracting pennies.
principles.quote: Github is apparently profitable, and it sounds like the people that work there spend their time trying to make the best service possible, _as opposed to spending their time trying to extract additional pennies out of their users_.

principles.text: Free services with vague business models trap founders: growth balloons costs, forcing a sale, ads, or endless fundraising.
principles.quote: Because the hosting bills and payroll balloon as the service grows, founders are left with a very difficult decision to make.

principles.text: Don't run an important service on hand-wavy promises of future monetization; it fails users, employees and trust.
principles.quote: Running a service that is important to people with some sort of hand-wavy platitudes about someday launching a “new form of advertising” is not OK.

principles.text: Pre-validate willingness to pay with an all-or-nothing campaign that only takes money at a defined critical mass.
principles.quote: We will only accept money for this financially sustainable, ad-free service if we hit what I believe is critical mass.

principles.text: A small base of 10,000 committed users can be a powerful starting position, so target the users who most want the product.
principles.quote: A search engine whose users consisted of the top 10,000 hackers and no one else would be in a very powerful position despite its small size, just as Google was when it was that size.
